Tech Report: Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • In a recent development, the premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface.
  • Industry observers note that to help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Driving at rush hour. SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. We’d come full circle: The bumper-to-bumper traffic that Miami, the city I once called home, is now notorious for — in no small part due to overdevelopment, climate change, and strained infrastructure — was being alleviated by a video game that keeps people at home, inside a simulation of the same city locked in time.

In a recent development, the premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface. The game follows Lucía Caminos and Jason Duval in the criminal underworld of Leonida, a fictionalized state based on South Florida: Miami becomes Vice City, the Everglades are the Grassrivers. But its portrayal of real-life hardships, socioeconomic inequality, and even Lucía and Jason’s love story, among other elements, has elicited deeper reflections and responses across our increasingly blurred online and physical worlds.

Industry observers note that to help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire. Castañeda is an artist and video game designer exploring Latin American Surrealism in the digital age, and soto co-leads Artists for Artists: Miami, which is leading a boycott of Art Basel next month, and works in the overlapping arenas of labor rights, public infrastructure, and conceptual and social practice.

According to recent reports, our conversation was edited and condensed for clarity. I hope you enjoy it.

Industry observers note that left: Leo Castañeda playing GTA VI, with a mural by Ahol Sniffs Glue included in the game. Right: misael soto's selfie in front of the inside of the clock tower in Assisi (photos courtesy the artists).

It has been revealed that hyperallergic: Before we even get into GTA, I was hoping each of you could tell me a little bit about your relationship to Miami — how long you've been there? How do you feel about living there now?

It has been revealed that leo Castañeda: I moved to Miami first when I was 11. My parents first moved to Fresh York [from Colombia], and then they thought it was too cold, so they moved to Miami. I went to middle school and high school here, then I moved to New York for college, and I moved back in 2015. When I first moved back after college, it was mostly because of the cost of living in New York. And then, within the 10 years that I've been here, it became the same cost of living as New York, except with Florida salaries.

I do feel grateful, though, to be part of the Bakehouse Art Complex, where I have an affordable studio. I live in the North Beach area, and I was able to find a sustainable rent. Miami has a lot of arts nonprofits that help over time. I do feel that, as complicated as the Miami arts ecosystem is, it is pretty supportive — but at the same time, it is tied to all the different layers of money that have come in and dominate the arts, which are very present here.

misael soto: I moved here right after undergrad. I grew up in South Florida, originally from Puerto Rico, and Miami was always la locura, down south. We would visit my cousins and whatnot from time to time. As I became more and more interested in starting my own practice, I moved down here and have continually been sucked back in. I try to leave, and it pulls me back for whatever reason. Since COVID, everything's changed. Miami became the second most expensive city in the country. The influx was palpable: All of a sudden, there were Texas and California and New York license plates, Teslas zipping around town, and rent just started skyrocketing. There's more flooding. But at the same time, it's gorgeous, and it's special. I live in Mid-Beach. I can go to the water, I can breathe in some sea air, I can hear 10 different languages at once.

It's a really complex relationship with Miami. Especially, I think, both of us make complicated art — we both make art that is unconventional and perhaps even, you could say, difficult to collect. I don't know if you describe yourself that way, Leo, but I definitely do. And making this kind of work in a hyper market-driven neoliberal city like Miami, on the one hand, it gives me a lot of fodder, a lot of material, a lot of things to talk about, as we're doing right now. But at the same time, it can be really frustrating and alienating and lonesome, ultimately.

According to recent reports, H: I moved from Argentina to Miami when I was little because my mom got a job there. We lived in the Doral neighborhood, where most people I knew were also from Latin America, until I left for Chicago for college at 18. I've lived in Latest York for over a decade now, but I still feel a strong pull to Miami, I feel seen, surrounded by people whose identities are a bit fractured the way I feel mine is.

In a recent development, and on the note of nostalgia, GTA is a game that was made over the last 13 years, so it chronicles a Miami that’s partly gone. For example, consumers say Lucía's home is based on a cute salmon-pink, 13-unit condo in Edgewater that was demolished in 2022 to build a 55-story tower, yet it lives on in the game. What does it mean for a video game to preserve a place that no longer exists?

LC: Well, a few thoughts. During that 13-year development, I would assume the map design was one of the first things they did. But there are also aspects of the chronicling of Miami, or Miami becoming this satire through the game, that have evolved in a shorter time period. For example, this morning I woke up, and there was a Miami Instagram influencer saying that in the fictional version of the Cuban coffee shop Versailles, which is called Antoinette, the bakery has a sign posted outside that claims something like, “any politician must pay for all the food when they leave.” That's a reference from a few years ago, when Trump reportedly went to Versailles, ordered food for everyone, and then didn't pay and just walked out.

So it does seem like a video game takes a long time to make, and this one is probably the most ambitious one ever made — 4,500 people working really, really hard, to the point of even having the union situations that they have in the UK branch of the company. But at the same time, I feel like they studied Miami extremely well, and the integration with some local businesses and local artists in particular — I've seen a few street artists like Ahol Sniffs Glue, Soak, Tatiana Suarez, Typoe, as well as musician Nick León. One restaurant is based on Juvia on Lincoln Road, which doesn't exist anymore — they got priced out, and now there's a record of it. The game takes so long to make, but it lives in an ever-present, because it doesn't matter if you made an asset 13 years in the past, like Lucía's apartment, or now; they feel like the present. It's an interesting amalgamation. I would have to spend more time with it to really know: Does this feel like Miami in 2014 or Miami in 2026, or a hybrid?

H: To get into the politics of the conversation around GTA, I have a lot of icky feelings about one narrative that's taking hold online, which is that the game is “Woke 3.0,” and that the incels and Trump supporters are pissed about it. I only played for a few hours last night, and I went into a gun shop and bought a shotgun. That, to me, panders much more to the NRA hawks and the pro-gun community than to anything that could be considered woke, you know?

MS: Hmm. I see it the other way around, actually. To me, it's like pretending in order to pacify, in some ways. It's a very complex thing. On the one hand, I remember seeing the woman twerking on the top of a car as the sun came up over the MacArthur. Now that's in the game. And I remember the “face eater” on the MacArthur. I see a man in a thong skateboarding weekly, and now there's a character like that in the game. I teach art history, and I do a whole week on postmodernism and poststructuralism and simulacrum, and the consequences of that, which I think have led us into some really dangerous flattening territory in terms of the role of the artist in the late 20th to early 21st century. I see this game and the way that it's taken over the city in real life and in gameplay, and it makes me think about how much of this is pacifying the role of the artist, or is it pushing through to the other end and becoming a meta-modernist critique that has some gems in there, if you're willing to find them?

Recent findings suggest that it ultimately makes me feel a bit sad in terms of what we deserve. I texted you yesterday, Valentina, when we were talking about having this conversation, and I said, “Well, maybe this is the kind of art the city deserves.” It's not the art that I want for Miami. But in so many ways, Miami is the perfect place. It's been the city for continual use by image makers, from Hollywood to video games.

In a recent development, H: There is some talk about the fact that the game does seem to have an awareness and sensitivity around identity. Cygnus, the curator at the Vice City Museum of Art, is the first non-binary character in Grand Theft Auto history. The actor cast for the role, Jesse James Rose, remarked that to prevent anti-trans violence, GTA made it so players would not be able to harm their character. Does this feel like an honest gesture, though?

It has been revealed that MS: I was just talking to a friend who's been playing it, and she was like, “Where are all the Haitians?” I remembered there was this huge lawsuit against GTA and Vice City, the one set in the ’80s, from about 20 years ago. Haitian groups sued Rockstar over their portrayal. I did some research, and it seems now the tech giant has shifted. They're saying, “We now punch up as opposed to punching down.” That feels, once again, so uncanny in comparison to the ways in which corporate America has shifted. It makes me think of the phrase, “Black faces in high places won't save us.” I don't want to be lobbing grenades at Rockstar. I think it's fantastic that these changes have been made, especially with such an influential game. But at the same time, it feels like the video game, in its attempt to replicate reality, is lagging in this area.

According to recent reports, H: GTA has a long history of racism. We shouldn't forget that Black characters have been associated with criminality throughout all editions of the game. I haven't played enough to say whether that's the case in the latest version. There is also the question of how the company actually treats its workers, and the labor disputes that are going on behind the scenes. Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer for Rockstar, wrote an opinion piece for the Guardian where he asked, why is it that with this game that generated billions of dollars, we are still fighting to get union recognition?

MS: I'm curious, Leo, as someone who has been playing games for as long as you have, how you feel about this. I'm a cinephile — I've been one since I was 18, and watched my first Kubrick film the summer before college. And I am dying to see Avengers: Doomsday (2026). I've been following the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) and have been consistently floored by the way they built out this world and the interconnected films. It's history, and it's been making history. But we all know how terrible Disney is. And even with the MCU, they tried to bring in more diversity, and the public didn't respond, so they backtracked on it. I don't know if that analogy holds. But it feels pertinent. It feels similar.

According to recent reports, LC: Of course, I have to play more to fully understand it. There's the ads of the game and the game itself. I would say that the Netflix special did feel like it was perpetuating some of the stereotypes of the Haitian community. But at the same time, having played, or seen the range of minority characters so far in the first couple hours, it feels like they have a wide range of personalities, body types, and interests. It's not like they're all criminals. And I also found out that local Haitian muralist Serge Toussaint has his work featured in the game, which I think is an amazing thing. But in terms of artworks in other mediums that really relate to this, this is kind of like, let's say, South Park, or Euphoria — demonstrates that are a mirror to the world that's very explicitly showing you both the best and the worst, and it's making fun of and critiquing everyone. But then how does it flip to show a new perspective or a solution?

Sources indicate that I've seen a lot of people, especially women game critics and game developers, celebrating the relationship of Jason and Lucía being a central situation in the game, as opposed to a cast of different men from different backgrounds, or, in GTA IV, the Eastern European guy in the seedy underground. Having the relationship and the cultivating of the relationship be a core mechanic, almost in a Sims-like way — and even the learning of emotional labor, or doing kind things around the house, or the game having a really interesting reward mechanic for the nonviolent interactions ... At least in my experience so far, three hours in, I haven't shot a single shot.

H: Wait, how did you save Donnie in the first mission without shooting people?

Sources indicate that LC: Oh, by hiding. It was saying, “Crouch around to make sure no one sees you.”.

Industry observers note that H: I think it's fascinating how different players can make these different decisions. I'm not very good at gaming, so I gave my husband the controller. I was like, “Get us out of here as quickly as possible. I want to get to Vice City!”.

LC: Yeah, and usually my criticism of Rockstar Games and also Naughty Dog, two big companies that have these cinematic, movie-like games, is that the story missions often have a path where you fail if you don't take a violent action. The emergent gameplay — which happens just by walking around, the dynamic gameplay that's not in a story mission — is usually extremely layered and nuanced and can go in any direction, violent or not. Again, I'm only three hours in with GTA VI, but so far I appreciate that it is giving the choice of not using violence, and kind of rewarding it. There's something interesting about that. Because usually in those Rockstar games, I'm like, okay, there's this emotional tale, and now there's a mission, and I have to kill 20 minions.

Sources indicate that MS: Leo, I'm thinking about your work and playing your pieces, immersing oneself in these worlds that you create, and there's a kind of mystery in the expansive potential that you create in your installations that at first can be a little overwhelming, but you have to just dive in. And this is the nature of games, or video games. There's a kind of trust fall. And I'm thinking about — let's just go there — the emancipatory potential of that. Because video games, to me, the potential in them as works is the building of awareness, the fostering of empathy, literally embodying someone who has a different way of life or a different body, a different perspective. Especially in our era of political correctness, and a lot of it is warranted, we're asked to speak from our own perspective and not assume things of others. And so this allowance — I wonder how you see the potential in that, especially in something like this game that is so immersive.

Sources indicate that LC: I think games as artworks are, to a certain extent, some of the most affordably accessible. Yes, you need to have a PC or PlayStation or Switch or something, but they could be pieces of art that are globally accessible in an immediate way, and they really can affect culture. In terms of empathy, you're controlling a being that you identify as “I”: “I” drove the boat today, or in my game, “I” was camouflaging with the environment to gain energy. There's something there about the mutability of the body, or how one could shift one's self-identity into multiple beings, that is interesting in games, and also interaction and choice as a place that could be art, in a way that performance art also does, and maybe theater. And visual arts in general, maybe in a less touch-based way. But in terms of the empathy, I've been seeing a lot of reviews of GTA VI saying it's actually leading people towards that. Perhaps it is through the romantic relationship [between Jason and Lucía], or maybe by having so much freedom to do whatever you want and kill whoever you want, but then developing these characters and NPCs to a level where they feel like real people.

Sources indicate that H: There is one moment in the game that was very emotive in a way that might provoke empathy, and it certainly did for me. At the very beginning — so this is not really a spoiler — we're shown the backstory of how Lucía gets arrested. She's been sitting at a cafe, a little Cuban cafecito, and she's just ordering ice water. The server keeps coming up to her and asking if she wants something else, and she's like, “No, no, just ice water for me.” It's clear that she just can't afford anything else. So in an act of true desperation, and from a place of deep poverty, she decides to rob a payday loan store nearby, and she gets caught. At one point, you can hear the cops saying, “She's saying she left something at the cafe.” And then we see the owners of the coffee shop taking care of her baby, who is then taken by social services.

We're not shown Tomás, her little baby, at the beginning. It's something that the game surprises us with. To me, it was such a thoughtfully articulated moment.

LC: The beginning is so strong. And then having the tutorial on how to walk and use the camera be her nine months later in prison. Out of overcapacity, the prison is letting some people who have lower sentences perhaps have probation, so she's gonna be let go, but the woman who works there says she doesn't know if or when Lucía will see her baby again. That works as a narrative tool, a teleology, giving purpose to the game beyond, “Oh, she's just a digital girlfriend.” Now there's this question of what the rewards of behavior are that the game's gonna have when one is part of the criminal underworld, but there is a child in foster care that could be taken back or not. That's gonna be so interesting if that ends up being a fork in the road within the narrative, because many of these games have multiple endings.

It has been revealed that MS: This is so fascinating to me in regards to something we were talking about earlier — whether reality is informing the simulacrum and vice versa. It makes me think of how, living in Miami, it continuously feels like maybe the most neoliberal city I've ever lived in. But in so many ways, it oftentimes feels like when you're on the road or when you're at a cafe, you're alone. You really have to fend for yourself in this city. Of course, there are these moments where you break through, or if you're a regular at Enriqueta's, you know who to talk to, this and that. It makes me wonder how the game might change the way that we see ourselves. And, following that thread, how might it actually make us more united?

I don't know if that's a bit of a stretch, but there are just so many people playing this game. And I think over time it's really going to show, as visitors come and reflect their years of gameplay back to the city. In the same way that folks experience Paris syndrome, what will the GTA Miami syndrome be? How might that change us? I was thinking about it for the worse, but how might it change us for the better? Because I don't know a Miami where that childcare situation in the GTA story would happen. Of course, I'm not a caregiver. I'm not a parent. But I don't know that Miami — and I've been here long enough and I have a lot of family here, chosen family. So that makes me, in a weird way, hopeful.

LC: I think it's interesting, let's say with Pop art and conceptual art — if you use a urinal or a fluorescent light, you think of urinal, Duchamp; fluorescent light, Dan Flavin, etc. These artists are claiming this thing from the world. And it's interesting to have this very fluid cycle of, let's say, the Only in Dade Instagram account becoming almost a live feed of GTA, or us within Miami filtering our experience — when there's a very special or odd moment, it being a rehearsal for the game, or the game getting reflected back in the world.

If the game is marketing itself as this debauched, wild place, and that lures millions and millions of people in, but then it ends up being this profound story that actually shows how South Florida has concerns of income inequality and climate change ... There's a hurricane system in the game, so there's a very strong chance that there will be flooding. Will that situation, where violence and comedy, or things that are not explicitly telling people what the values should be, actually make them more subtle and implicit? Does that create change or not?

According to recent reports, H: We've been speaking over an hour, we could probably talk for two more hours. This feels like a beautiful note to end on. But I want to ask if there are any burning observations you want to share.

Sources indicate that MS: I feel like we should speak about the takeover of Miami in the real world, physically. Today is Dezeen’s 20th birthday, and to celebrate we launch our 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler.

For the series we’ve asked 20 architects and designers who have had a major impact over the past 20 years to each select an architect or designer that they believe will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years.

Called 20×20, the project aims to celebrate the past 20 years of Dezeen while looking forward to the names and faces we’ll be seeing much more of in the next 20 years.

We’ll be revealing the selected architects and designers on Dezeen over the next four weeks, getting to know them and their work in a series of interviews.

The series launches today with a profile of Russian-born, Paris-based designer Harry Nuriev, who was selected by Danish architect Bjarke Ingels.

He will be followed by the selections of Es Devlin, Faye Toogood, Francine Houbine, Frida Escobedo, Huberto Campana, Iris van herpen, Jeanne Gang, Kelly Wearstler, Lesley Lokko, Ma Yansong, Marc Newson, Mariam Kamara, Marina Tabassum, Nendo, Neri&Hu, Patricia Urquiola, Sabine Marcelis, Sou Fujimoto and Yasmeen Lari.

All of the interviews will be listed below as they are published:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Lucas Blair Simpson.

Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia, USA, “breathing new life” into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.

The project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns. It serves as a major transit hub for the Northeastern United States.

The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.

Keeping to the historic details, including the art deco chandeliers that hang from the tall ceilings, SOM restored the space with builder Gilbane through renovation and a series of specific interventions.

Chief among these was the moving of ticketing, bag drop-off, and other facilities that had been placed in the main train hall into a little-used northern wing of the building.

“Our restoration and repositioning presents an extraordinary opportunity to leverage the station’s strengths, while breathing newly introduced life into this beloved building,” remarked SOM Partner Colin Koop.

This move freed up more room for seating and through traffic in the main hall.

Working with retail partner Nelson Worldwide, SOM also revamped the concessions in the south concourse.

SOM worked closely with US rail system operator Amtrak on the project, which includes offices for Amtrak in the upper levels of the building.

It is part of a wider renovation SOM unveiled for the station and surrounding areas in Philadelphia in 2016, which included a number of tall buildings. The status of these new structures is unclear.

SOM noted the efforts in preserving the character of the structure.

“We are preserving its historic character while positioning the station for the next generation of travelers to come,” stated SOM Principal Phil Wessell.

“As part of our broader work along Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor, this revitalization reinforces the station’s role as both a vital transportation hub and a defining civic space for Philadelphia.”.

SOM also led the renovation of Daniel Patrick Moynihan Train Hall in Newly introduced York in 2021, with prepares for a Penn Station renovation released earlier this year by PAU.

Photography by Lucas Blair Simpson.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

It has been revealed that picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Château Léoville Barton in hand, watching the Australian coastline slowly materialize through your window. The cabin is hushed. The seat — Cathay Pacific's renowned Business Class throne on the Airbus A350-1000 — cocoons you in a private pod with a sliding door, direct aisle access, and a mattress pad that makes a five-star hotel bed feel like an afterthought. This is the LAX–HKG–SYD route in Cathay Pacific Business Class. And you booked it for 55,000 Alaska Mileage Blueprint miles. Now consider what the person three rows up in economy paid in cash for their seat — and what the couple beside you in business paid for theirs. A Cathay Pacific Business Class ticket on this route typically retails between **$5,000 and $12,000**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin pricing on transpacific routes is notoriously aggressive, and Australia amplifies it further because of the sheer distance involved. At 55,000 miles for a one-way business class redemption, you're extracting somewhere between **9.1 and 21.8 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that makes most loyalty program strategists stop and stare. Alaska Mileage Strategy is one of the most valuable frequent flyer programs in the world despite being a relatively small airline. Breaking: National Gallery of Canada receives major gift of modern and contemporary glass art

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a latest chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman.
  • Sources indicate that “This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper.
  • Industry observers note that the gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a latest chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman. Accompanied by an endowment to establish the institution’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design, the donation will help broaden the museum’s collection and increase its scholarly contributions.

Sources indicate that “This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper. “It significantly expands our understanding of art history, bringing together artistic expression and material and technical innovation.”.

Industry observers note that the gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia. The collection traces the medium’s evolution from the sinuous forms of Art Nouveau and Arts and Crafts to the streamlined aesthetics of Art Deco and Modernism. Early 20th-century examples by Tiffany Studios, Émile Gallé and the renowned studio Daum demonstrate how artists pushed glass beyond traditional decorative applications.

Daum Frères, Lamp, around 1905. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC.

Recent findings suggest that the works also chart the emergence of studio glass as an independent discipline in the post-war period. Additional artists with works in the donation include Dale Chihuly, whose gravity-defying installations are in museums worldwide, as well as the studio glass pioneer Toots Zynsky and the well-known Canadian American artist Laura Donefer.

According to recent reports, A selection of pieces from the collection is currently on view in the NGC’s European galleries (until 30 April 2027). Highlights of the installation include Edward Hald’s The Fireworks Bowl (around 1921), alongside architectural works by Tiffany and Frank Lloyd Wright.

“Harvey Littleton’s Red Crossed Form (1990) is another notable work that reflects the development of studio glass as an independent artistic medium,” says Anabelle Kienle Ponka, the NGC’s senior curator of European, American and Asian Art. “The presentation brings together very different approaches to glass, from the decorative traditions of the early 20th century to the formal and technical experimentation of contemporary artists.”.

It has been revealed that tiffany Studios, Lamp, around 1900. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC.

The international scope of the donation highlights the exchange of technical traditions, particularly the influence of Venetian glassmaking on successive generations of artists, Kienle Ponka says. Together, the works demonstrate the medium’s versatility across sculpture, architecture and ornamentation.

Equally significant for the NGC is the accompanying endowment, which will fund the museum’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design. The NGC has not shared the sum of the endowment, but notes that the post will support research, exhibitions and future acquisitions, establishing a foundation for sustained institutional engagement with the field.

“[The donation’s] significance extends well beyond this gift,” Bélisle states. “The position will allow us to pursue further acquisitions, develop exhibitions and scholarship, and build relationships with artists and institutions.”.

Installation view of works by Lino Tagliapietra and Harvey Littleton from the Bronfman Glass Collection, National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa, until 30 April 2027. Photo: National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa.

Sources indicate that the donation builds on a long history of the Bronfman family’s philanthropy in Canada's cultural sector. “My late wife Andy and I were admirers of the art of glass making and wanted to share this love with other Canadians,” Charles Bronfman mentioned in a statement. “With the planned celebrations marking the upcoming 100th birthday of my sister, Phyllis Lambert, founder of the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and the 50th anniversary of the Canada Council for the Arts’ Saidye Bronfman Award, named after my mother, I am truly delighted to be contributing in this meaningful way to the national collections.”.

The NGC has received other transformative gifts in recent years, including a 2025 donation of 61 contemporary works valued at C$22.8m ($16.8m) from collector Bob Rennie and his family. “The Bronfman gift is significant in a different way,” Bélisle says. “Its importance lies not only in the quality and range of the works, but also in the accompanying endowment, which will provide the expertise and resources to develop decorative arts and design as a sustained area of collecting and scholarship.”.

  • Perron overhauled the kitchen for a longstanding client, with whom the studio has worked on several professional and personal projects over the years.
  • Her residence sits along the south shore of the St Lawrence River, overlooking Quebec City on the opposite bank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Paul Dussault.

A dedicated space for preparing tea has been placed at the heart of this Canadian house’s renovated kitchen, designed by local studio Perron.

Perron overhauled the kitchen for a longstanding client, with whom the studio has worked on several professional and personal projects over the years.

Her residence sits along the south shore of the St Lawrence River, overlooking Quebec City on the opposite bank.

The view across the water, and the client’s love of tea, were the primary guiding elements for the renovation project.

“For this house, we were not simply working from a checklist of requirements,” mentioned Perron founder Nathalie Perron.

“We already knew about our client’s lifestyle, energy and the things that are most important to her.”.

The kitchen space was divided into three zones: a space for tea, a central cooking area and a counter overlooking the river.

At the entrance, a small counter wrapped in glossy oxblood red tiles and a partition of burgundy steel bars form a niche that the client has nicknamed her “teahouse”.

Custom lacquered MDF wall shelves store and display cups, saucers, mugs and teapots that she has collected during her travels over the years.

“Each one evokes a specific memory and now has a place in her daily life,” said Perron.

An on-demand hot water tap is also installed within this niche, creating a dedicated space for the tea-making ritual.

The main kitchen area revolves around an angular island, which has space for a bar stool and incorporates a built-in electric stove.

Above, a cylindrical burgundy-hued range hood is framed within more steel bars, suspended from the ceiling to support shelves.

Rows of glass blocks are stacked between the upper and lower cabinets, which are both faced in stained white oak.

Ultra-thin steel shelves hang from the upper millwork, adding extra storage without blocking the light through the translucent bricks.

Opposite, a long counter faces the river through a large window, allowing the homeowner to witness passing ships and changing light conditions as she stands working or washing dishes.

Cristallo quartzite from Brazil forms the countertop and a backsplash.

Long, narrow Cotto Manetti terracotta tiles cover the floor, echoing the shapes of the matte and gloss pink Farblok ceramic tiles by Quintessenza that run up the wall in stripes.

A Mousse wall fixture by Quebec lighting brand JETA adds another feminine touch to the kitchen.

“It is a house that reflects a woman who enjoys going on adventures, but who has created a home that she loves returning to,” said the studio.

Perron has offices in Montreal and Quebec, the latter in an early 20th-century building renovated to house a studio, showroom and Nathalie Perron’s home.

#45788. Canva's 'AI off switch' finally recognises the backlash from creatives

Canva's 'AI off switch' finally recognises the backlash from creatives

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that over the past couple of years, most of the press releases coming from software companies have contained announcements of new AI features.
  • Sources indicate that canva is one of those companies, and it's introduced a bunch of generative AI tools to its design platform.
  • Canva has added two AI controls for both Free and Pro customers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that over the past couple of years, most of the press releases coming from software companies have contained announcements of new AI features. Image, video and vector generation, removal tools, agentic workflows, AI assistants, and myriad other advances that can help artists do in seconds something that used to take hours.

Sources indicate that canva is one of those companies, and it's introduced a bunch of generative AI tools to its design platform. So the email I received yesterday made me do a double take. On the day that Anthropic completed the world's biggest IPO in history, it introduced an 'AI off switch'.

Canva has added two AI controls for both Free and Pro customers. The generative AI switch can be used to hide all of its generative AI tools, including Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Expand, Dream Lab and Canva Code. It can be switched on or off at any time.

According to recent reports, there's also an option to “See less AI content” on Canva's library of templates and design elements. This addresses complaints about the glut of AI-generated content making it harder to find quality work, something that's been causing problems on platforms as varied as Etsy and ArtStation.

Canva notes AI-generated content remains a "small portion" of its library and that such content is identified in its metadata. Turning on the latest function isn't guaranteed to remove it completely, but it should put human-made templates and design elements first in search results and recommendations.

The addition of a couple of toggles to the UI wouldn't normally be breaking news, so the fact that Canva feels this deserved its own announcement is telling. After heavily promoting AI tools, it's now presenting the ability to turn them off as a groundbreaking advance – and it is. This might be the first time that a major AI-forward creative software developer has recognised that a sizable portion of its user base just isn't into it.

In a recent development, "We believe AI has extraordinary potential to help people bring their ideas to life, and we're excited to keep pushing the boundaries of what's possible," Canva claims. "At the same time, like so many of you, we know there's something special about the time, care, and creativity that goes into making something that's truly yours.".

Industry observers note that an 'AI off button' is something that some creatives have been calling for. Part of the difficulty in implementing one is that it needs a definition of AI. Programs like Adobe's Photoshop have used machine learning for many years; it just wasn't branded as 'AI'. Many artists welcome tools that speed up their work, but not ones that do the creation part for them, especially if they're powered by models that were trained on unlicensed work.

Canva's recognised that. The toggle only turns off generative AI tools, such as ones that generate upcoming imagery, text or code from prompts. Assistive editing tools like Background Remover or Magic Grab, which lets you select and move an object in an image will still be available. Using them won't cause your work to be shamed with metadata identifying it as AI-generated.

Sources indicate that A 'no AI button' also requires a willingness from the provider. Since generative AI features are often charged on a per-use basis via credits, software companies generally want to encourage their customers to use them.

Adobe teased some impressive-looking AI-powered tools in the Adobe Max Sneaks presentation last week, but it's also clear that some customers detest generative AI, which has created a market for latest tools like the artist-led Niva app, which is promoting itself as AI-free art software.

Will an AI-off button let Canva have its cake and eat it?

You can learn more about Canva on the website.
